transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Good afternoon, both. Thanks for coming. Today we need to settle the topic for your technology presentation, so let's hear your first ideas. Priya, would you like to start?

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Yes, thanks, Dr Carter. I'd like to look at smartphone apps for language learning. I use three of them myself, so I already know quite a lot about how they work.

transcript.speaker: S3
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm not convinced. There are hundreds of studies on that already, and I think we'd only repeat what everyone says. I'd prefer something local, like the new electric buses in our city.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Marcus, that's a fair point about apps, but I'm worried about buses too. Remember that the presentation is only ten minutes long, and the council hasn't published much yet, so you might struggle to find enough information.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: I see what you mean. Perhaps we could combine the two ideas, but I'm not sure how.

transcript.speaker: S3
transcript.text: Well, what about studying how students really use technology for their courses? We could interview twenty people on campus. It sounds simple, but at least the data would be ours.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: That's a much more promising direction. However, you would need ethical approval before you speak to anyone, and that usually takes about three weeks.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Three weeks? That's too long. We have to present on the twelfth of November, and that's only a month away.

transcript.speaker: S3
transcript.text: Right. In that case, we could send out an online questionnaire instead. Doesn't that only need a short form?

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Exactly. A questionnaire needs only a short form, and approval normally comes back within a few days.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: Great. I'll draft the questions tonight. Do you have any advice about how to write them?

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Two things. Keep them short, and keep the wording neutral. If you ask, Don't you agree that apps are very useful, you're pushing people towards one answer, and the results will mean very little.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: That makes sense. When should I send you the draft?

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: By Friday, please. No, wait, I'm at a conference on Friday, so make it Thursday morning.

transcript.speaker: S3
transcript.text: That's fine. One thing still worries me, though. Even with neutral questions, mostly students who enjoy technology will reply, so our results could look more positive than they really are.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Quite. That's a form of bias, and it's worth discussing in your conclusion. Don't treat it as a failure, though. Examiners value honesty about limitations far more than a perfect-looking study.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: So we'd say our findings are suggestive, rather than conclusive?

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Precisely. And if your sample is small, avoid words like prove or show. Something like the data points towards is much safer, and it also sounds more professional.
